title: 2027 economic outlook: Resilience to continue, but the risks are building
gist: Oxford Economics expects global growth resilience to persist into 2027 but has trimmed its forecast to a 2.8%-3.0% GDP range, flagging oil-market stress around the Strait of Hormuz and a slower, more volatile phase of the AI boom as the two swing factors that could end the cycle.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics forecasts global GDP growth moving back into a 2.8% to 3.0% range for 2027, a markdown from prior forecasts driven by rising oil-market and AI-boom risks.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A sub-3% global growth print is the base case investors should model for 2027, not a reacceleration; treat prior above-3% forecasts as stale.
insights.quote: Overall, we forecast global GDP growth to move back into the 2.8% to 3.0% range.
insights.locator: Overall, we forecast global GDP growth

insights.claim: Oxford Economics remains more upbeat on the US growth outlook than consensus, but this above-consensus view does not extend to other major economies.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: US-specific outperformance versus consensus is a differentiated call worth tracking against incoming US data, but investors should not extrapolate the same optimism to Europe, China or other major economies.
insights.quote: We retain a relatively upbeat assessment of the US outlook versus the consensus expectation, but by and large, this doesn’t read-across into above-consensus forecasts for other major economies.
insights.locator: We retain a relatively upbeat assessment

insights.claim: The global economy proved remarkably resilient to a swathe of geopolitical shocks in 2026, and Oxford Economics expects that resilience to continue into 2027.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Baseline expectation should be continued economic resilience despite headline geopolitical noise, arguing against over-hedging portfolios purely on geopolitical headlines.
insights.quote: The global economy has again proven remarkably resilient to a swathe of geopolitical shocks in 2026, and we can expect that to continue into 2027.
insights.locator: The global economy has again proven

insights.claim: A major economic downturn would require a specific trigger event rather than emerging from current trend conditions alone.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Frames the 2027 risk case as event-driven (oil shock or AI-bust catalyst) rather than a base-case recession, useful for scenario-weighting portfolio hedges.
insights.quote: A major downturn would need a trigger.
insights.locator: A major downturn would need a trigger

themes.theme: Oil Market and Strait of Hormuz Risk

insights.claim: Global oil supply and the oil price are identified as one of the key swing factors determining whether growth rebounds in 2027.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Oil price trajectory is a primary macro variable to monitor as a leading indicator for the 2027 growth path.
insights.quote: One of the key determinants of whether growth will rebound next year is what happens to global oil supply and, by extension, the oil price.

insights.claim: The most likely oil-market scenario is continued simmering US-Iran tensions with lower-than-normal shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz persisting until at least the end of 2027.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Investors should expect a prolonged (multi-year) period of constrained Hormuz throughput as the base case, not a near-term resolution, when pricing energy and shipping/insurance exposure.
insights.quote: We now consider the most likely scenario to be simmering tensions between the US and Iran and lower-than-normal traffic in the Strait of Hormuz until at least the end of 2027.
insights.locator: We now consider the most likely scenario

insights.claim: Even with reduced Strait of Hormuz traffic persisting into 2027, Oxford Economics does not expect this to necessarily push oil prices sharply higher.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Decouples the intuitive link between constrained Hormuz shipping and higher oil prices, suggesting energy-price spike hedges tied to Hormuz disruption may be overpriced relative to Oxford Economics' base case.
insights.quote: However, this needn’t result in oil prices ratcheting higher.
insights.locator: However, this needn’t result in oil prices

insights.claim: Concerns about the scale of hyperscalers' liabilities combined with growing competition from Chinese AI firms signal a new phase of the AI boom characterized by slower investment growth and more volatile stock prices.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Investors in AI infrastructure and hyperscaler equities should expect a regime shift toward slower capex growth and higher volatility rather than a straight-line continuation of 2024-2026 AI capex trends.
insights.quote: Meanwhile, worries about the scale of hyperscalers’ liabilities and growing competition from Chinese AI firms point to a new phase in the AI boom: slower investment growth and more volatile stock prices.

insights.claim: A slower, more volatile AI investment phase would reduce the support AI capex provides to overall economic growth, but this does not automatically mean the AI boom turns into a bust.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Positions AI-driven GDP support as a fading but not collapsing tailwind for 2027 growth forecasts; a bust scenario requires an additional trigger beyond slower investment growth alone.
insights.quote: That would reduce the support AI provides to economic growth, but it doesn’t automatically follow that the boom will turn to bust.
insights.locator: That would reduce the support AI provides

insights.claim: A disorderly end to the AI investment boom is explicitly named as one of the two scenarios (alongside oil market stress) that could end the current economic cycle.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Frames AI-capex unwind risk as a top-tier macro tail risk on par with an oil shock, warranting monitoring of hyperscaler capex guidance and credit spreads as early-warning indicators.
insights.quote: Still, risks that oil market stress or a disorderly end to the AI boom could end the economic cycle are growing, and we’ve marked down our growth forecasts for 2027.
insights.locator: Still, risks that oil market stress

insights.claim: Oxford Economics maintains a longstanding view that the impact of geopolitical shocks on economic activity is generally overstated, even while acknowledging further geopolitical instability could still act as a downturn trigger.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A durable house view to weigh against headline-driven geopolitical risk-off trades: Oxford Economics argues geopolitical scares tend to be overpriced relative to their actual growth impact.
insights.quote: Further geopolitical instability could be the catalyst, but we’ve long argued that the impact of geopolitical shocks on economic activity is overstated.
insights.locator: Further geopolitical instability could be the catalyst
